notes.front: What is reasonable cause, as a ground for penalty relief?
notes.back: Acting with ordinary care and good faith yet still failing to comply; it can remove or reduce certain penalties.
notes.explanation: The IRS page says certain penalties may be removed or reduced when the taxpayer acted with reasonable cause and in good faith, judged case by case on all the facts.
notes.example: Like a landlord waiving a late-rent fee for a tenant who was in hospital on the due date, but decided by the IRS for a tax penalty.
notes.source: IRS, “Penalty relief due to reasonable cause”, “Reasonable cause”
notes.evidence: You may qualify to have certain penalties removed or reduced if you acted with reasonable cause and in good faith.

notes.front: What is First Time Abate (FTA)?
notes.back: The IRS’s most common administrative penalty waiver, for taxpayers with three years of timely compliance history.
notes.explanation: It rests on the taxpayer’s record of timely compliance rather than on a reason for the failure.
notes.example: Like a library forgiving the first overdue fine for a member who has returned every book on time for years.
notes.source: IRS, “Penalty relief due to First Time Abate or other administrative waiver”, “First Time Abate (FTA)”
notes.evidence: The most common administrative penalty waiver provided by the IRS, First Time Abate (FTA), applies to taxpayers with three years of timely compliance history.

notes.front: What is Automatic Exemption from Penalty (AEP)?
notes.back: The relief replacing FTA from summer 2026: late filers or payers with three clean prior years are simply not assessed the penalty.
notes.explanation: The IRS page says AEP begins in summer 2026 and covers 2025 tax year returns onward, with no request needed. It is IRS practice adopted after the exam's 31 December 2025 cut-off, so the exam is likely to test FTA.
notes.example: Like a toll road that stops sending a late-payment fee to drivers with a clean record, rather than sending it and refunding it on request.
notes.source: IRS, “Penalty relief due to First Time Abate or other administrative waiver”, “Automatic Exemption from Penalty (AEP)”
notes.evidence: Under AEP, if you file or pay late in the current year but have timely filed returns and paid tax due for the three prior years (or 12 consecutive quarters for quarterly filers), you won’t be assessed a penalty.

notes.front: What is a ministerial act, for interest abatement?
notes.back: A procedural or mechanical IRS act, involving no judgment or discretion, done after all its prerequisites have taken place.
notes.explanation: A decision on how tax law applies is never a ministerial act, however routine it looks.
notes.example: Like a clerk posting a signed court order to the file: the decision is already made, only the paperwork remains.
notes.source: IRS, “Interest abatement”, “Ministerial act”
notes.evidence: A ministerial act is a procedural or mechanical act that does not involve the exercise of judgment or discretion, and that occurs during the processing of a taxpayer’s case after all prerequisites to the act, such as conferences and review by supervisors, have taken place.

notes.front: What is a managerial act, for interest abatement?
notes.back: An administrative act in processing a case that involves losing records or using judgment in managing personnel.
notes.explanation: The definition covers two things only: lost records and personnel decisions; a decision on applying tax law is excluded.
notes.example: Like a shop manager deciding to leave a till unstaffed while its cashier is on a course, so the queue waits.
notes.source: IRS, “Interest abatement”, “Managerial act”
notes.evidence: A managerial act is an administrative act that occurs during the processing of a taxpayer's case involving the temporary or permanent loss of records or the exercise of judgment or discretion relating to management of personnel.

notes.front: Who is a federally authorized tax practitioner under section 7525?
notes.back: An individual authorised under federal law to practise before the IRS, where that practice is regulated under 31 U.S.C. 330.
notes.explanation: Two things are needed: federal authority to practise before the IRS, and regulation of that practice under section 330 of title 31.
notes.example: Like a solicitor’s client privilege, but extended to an enrolled agent advising on a tax matter.
notes.source: 26 U.S.C. § 7525, Confidentiality privileges relating to taxpayer communications, “(a)(3)(A) Federally authorized tax practitioner”
notes.evidence: The term "federally authorized tax practitioner" means any individual who is authorized under Federal law to practice before the Internal Revenue Service if such practice is subject to Federal regulation under section 330 of title 31, United States Code.

notes.front: What is the burden of proof in a tax court case?
notes.back: The duty to prove a disputed factual issue; under section 7491 it can shift to the IRS when the taxpayer brings credible evidence.
notes.explanation: Section 7491(a) moves the burden to the Secretary for a factual issue once the taxpayer introduces credible evidence, subject to its conditions.
notes.example: Like a referee who makes the other side disprove a claim once one side has produced a credible receipt.
notes.source: 26 U.S.C. § 7491, Burden of proof, “(a)(1) General rule”
notes.evidence: If, in any court proceeding, a taxpayer introduces credible evidence with respect to any factual issue relevant to ascertaining the liability of the taxpayer for any tax imposed by subtitle A or B, the Secretary shall have the burden of proof with respect to such issue.

notes.front: What is a 30-day letter?
notes.back: The letter sent after an examination telling the taxpayer of the right to appeal the proposed changes within 30 days.
notes.explanation: Publication 556 says it arrives in a package a few weeks after the closing conference with the examiner or supervisor.
notes.example: Like a written decision that gives you a month to lodge an appeal before it becomes final.
notes.source: Publication 556, Examination of Returns, Appeal Rights, and Claims for Refund (Rev. September 2013), “30-day letter and 90-day letter”, p. 5
notes.evidence: A letter (known as a 30-day letter) notifying you of

notes.front: What is the Independent Office of Appeals?
notes.back: The IRS function, separate from the division that proposed the changes, that settles tax disputes without litigation.
notes.explanation: Publication 5 states its mission as resolving tax controversies without litigation, fairly and impartially to both sides.
notes.example: Like an ombudsman inside a company who reviews a department’s decision without answering to that department.
notes.source: Publication 5, Your Appeal Rights and How To Prepare a Protest If You Disagree (Rev. 4-2021), “The IRS Independent Office of Appeals Mission”, p. 1
notes.evidence: To resolve Federal tax controversies without litigation on a basis which is fair and impartial to both the Government and the taxpayer

notes.front: What is a protest, in an IRS dispute?
notes.back: A written statement of disagreement that a taxpayer submits to request an Appeals conference.
notes.explanation: Publication 5 says the Appeals employee uses the protest to prepare for the conference.
notes.example: Like a written grounds-of-appeal document filed before a hearing, but addressed to IRS Appeals.
notes.source: Publication 5, Your Appeal Rights and How To Prepare a Protest If You Disagree (Rev. 4-2021), “Protests”, p. 3
notes.evidence: You must submit a written protest to request

notes.front: What is a small case request?
notes.back: A simpler request for Appeals, allowed instead of a formal written protest when tax and penalties per period are $25,000 or less (Pub 5, 2021).
notes.explanation: Publication 5 counts the proposed increase or decrease in tax, including penalties, or the claimed refund, for each period.
notes.example: Like a small-claims form that replaces a full statement of case when the sum in dispute is modest.
notes.source: Publication 5, Your Appeal Rights and How To Prepare a Protest If You Disagree (Rev. 4-2021), “Small Case Request”, p. 3
notes.evidence: tax period involved is $25,000 or less in the letter

notes.front: What is a notice of deficiency?
notes.back: The IRS notice, sent by certified or registered mail, that determines a deficiency; also called the 90-day letter.
notes.explanation: Section 6212(a) also requires the notice to tell the taxpayer of the right to contact a local taxpayer advocate office.
notes.example: Like a formal demand letter that also starts the clock for going to court.
notes.source: 26 U.S.C. § 6212, Notice of deficiency, “(a) In general”
notes.evidence: he is authorized to send notice of such deficiency to the taxpayer by certified mail or registered mail. Such notice shall include a notice to the taxpayer of the taxpayer's right to contact a local office of the taxpayer advocate

notes.front: Reasonable cause does not apply to certain penalties, such as the {{c1::estimated tax}} penalty.
notes.explanation: The IRS page points taxpayers to separate rules for reducing the estimated tax penalty.
notes.source: IRS, “Penalty relief due to reasonable cause”, “Reasonable cause”
notes.evidence: Reasonable cause doesn't apply to certain penalties such as the estimated tax penalty.

notes.front: What are two examples of reasons that may be valid reasonable cause for filing or paying late?
notes.back: Any two of: fire, natural disaster or civil disturbance; inability to get records; death, serious illness or unavoidable absence; system issues.
notes.explanation: The IRS lists these as examples, so the list is open; Policy Statement 3-2 gives more detail.
notes.source: IRS, “Penalty relief due to reasonable cause”, “Failure to file or pay penalties”
notes.evidence: Examples of valid reasons for failing to file or pay on time may include: Fires, natural disasters or civil disturbances Inability to get records Death, serious illness or unavoidable absence of the taxpayer or immediate family System issues that delayed a timely electronic filing or payment

notes.front: Is relying on a tax professional generally reasonable cause for filing or paying late?
notes.back: No. The taxpayer stays responsible even when someone else handles the taxes.
notes.explanation: The IRS expects taxpayers to know what their preparer files and to get proof that the return or payment was sent on time.
notes.source: IRS, “Penalty relief due to reasonable cause”, “Failure to file or pay penalties”
notes.evidence: Reliance on a tax professional. You're generally responsible for complying with tax law even if someone else handles your taxes. You should know what your tax preparer files and get proof that your return or payment is sent on time.

notes.front: Is lack of funds reasonable cause for failing to pay tax?
notes.back: Not by itself, though other facts showing reasonable care and an attempt to comply may qualify.
notes.explanation: The IRS keeps the door open: lack of funds alone fails, but it can sit alongside other circumstances.
notes.source: IRS, “Penalty relief due to reasonable cause”, “Failure to file or pay penalties”
notes.evidence: By itself, lack of funds is not reasonable cause for failing to pay or deposit taxes due. However, you may qualify for relief based on other facts and circumstances that show you used reasonable care and tried to comply with tax law.

notes.front: What are two factors the IRS weighs for reasonable cause relief from an accuracy-related penalty?
notes.back: Any two of: efforts to report correctly; complexity of the issue; the taxpayer’s education, experience or knowledge; steps to understand or seek advice.
notes.explanation: The IRS says it considers factors “including” these, so other factors may count too.
notes.source: IRS, “Penalty relief due to reasonable cause”, “Accuracy-related penalties”
notes.evidence: Efforts you made to report the correct tax The complexity of the tax issue Your education, experience, or knowledge of tax law Steps you took to understand your tax obligation or seek help from a tax advisor

notes.front: If penalty relief cannot be approved by phone, how can the taxpayer request it in writing?
notes.back: On Form 843, Claim for Refund and Request for Abatement.
notes.explanation: Form 843 is the written route when the taxpayer qualifies for neither relief over the phone.
notes.source: IRS, “Penalty relief due to reasonable cause”, “How to request penalty relief”
notes.evidence: If you don't qualify for either or we can't approve your relief over the phone, you can request relief in writing with Form 843, Claim for Refund and Request for Abatement.

notes.front: What happens to the interest on a penalty when the IRS removes or reduces that penalty?
notes.back: The IRS automatically reduces or removes the related interest.
notes.explanation: The IRS charges interest on penalties, and says it adjusts that interest automatically when a penalty is reduced or removed.
notes.source: IRS, “Penalty relief due to reasonable cause”, “Interest relief”
notes.evidence: We'll automatically reduce or remove the related interest if we reduce or remove any of your penalties.

notes.front: Must a taxpayer name FTA or send documents when asking for it?
notes.back: No. The taxpayer must contact the IRS, but need not specify FTA or provide supporting documents.
notes.explanation: The IRS checks the account history itself to see whether the FTA requirements are met.
notes.source: IRS, “Penalty relief due to First Time Abate or other administrative waiver”, “First Time Abate (FTA)”
notes.evidence: Though taxpayers must contact the IRS to request this relief, you don’t need to specify FTA as the relief sought or provide supporting documents in your request for relief. The IRS will review your account information to see if you meet the requirements for FTA.

notes.front: Which failure-to-file penalties can FTA relieve?
notes.back: Failure to file tax returns (section 6651(a)(1)), partnership returns (6698(a)(1)) and S corporation returns (6699(a)(1)).
notes.explanation: The IRS lists these under “Failure to File”, eligible regardless of amount.
notes.source: IRS, “Penalty relief due to First Time Abate or other administrative waiver”, “Penalties eligible for relief”
notes.evidence: Failure to File Tax returns – IRC 6651(a)(1) Partnership returns – IRC 6698(a)(1) S corporation returns – IRC 6699(a)(1)

notes.front: Which failure-to-pay penalties can FTA relieve?
notes.back: Section 6651(a)(2), tax shown not paid by the due date, and 6651(a)(3), tax that should have been shown not paid by the notice date.
notes.explanation: Both are listed under “Failure to Pay” on the IRS page of eligible penalties.
notes.source: IRS, “Penalty relief due to First Time Abate or other administrative waiver”, “Penalties eligible for relief”
notes.evidence: When the tax shown on the return is not paid by the due date – IRC 6651(a)(2) When the tax is required to be shown on a return, but was not, and that tax was not paid by the date stated in the notice or demand for payment – IRC 6651(a)(3)

notes.front: Which Code section’s deposit penalty can FTA relieve?
notes.back: Section 6656, failure to deposit tax in the correct amount, on time or in the required manner.
notes.explanation: It is the third family on the IRS list, beside failure to file and failure to pay.
notes.source: IRS, “Penalty relief due to First Time Abate or other administrative waiver”, “Penalties eligible for relief”
notes.evidence: When the tax was not deposited in the correct amount, within the prescribed time period, and/or in the required manner – IRC 6656

notes.front: Under FTA, what filing history must the taxpayer have for the same return type?
notes.back: Timely filing for the prior three years (or 12 consecutive quarters).
notes.explanation: This is the first part of the “timely compliance history” the IRS requires.
notes.source: IRS, “Penalty relief due to First Time Abate or other administrative waiver”, “How to qualify for the relief”
notes.evidence: The same return type, as the original return, was timely filed for the prior three years (or 12 consecutive quarters)

notes.front: Under FTA, which prior penalty does not spoil a clean history?
notes.back: The estimated tax penalty; a penalty later abated for reasonable cause or IRS error also does not count.
notes.explanation: Otherwise no penalty may have been assessed in the look-back period.
notes.source: IRS, “Penalty relief due to First Time Abate or other administrative waiver”, “How to qualify for the relief”
notes.evidence: Either no penalty (except the estimated tax penalty) was assessed or a penalty was assessed, but later abated for reasonable cause or IRS error

notes.front: Under section 6404(f), when will the IRS abate a penalty caused by its own erroneous written advice?
notes.back: Only if the taxpayer reasonably relied on it, it answered a specific written request, and the taxpayer gave adequate, accurate information.
notes.explanation: The Form 843 instructions list these three conditions and refer to Regulations section 301.6404-3.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 843 (Rev. December 2024), “Requesting Abatement or Refund of a Penalty or Addition to Tax as a Result of Written Advice”, p. 4
notes.evidence: The written advice was in response to a specific written

notes.front: Under section 6404(e)(1), when may the IRS reduce interest a taxpayer owes?
notes.back: When the interest arises from an IRS officer or employee’s unreasonable error or delay.
notes.explanation: The IRS page notes that interest itself is required by statute; 6404(e)(1) gives relief only for interest caused by the IRS.
notes.source: IRS, “Interest abatement”, “Interest abatement”
notes.evidence: Interest is required by statute, but the IRS may reduce the amount of interest you owe if the interest is applied because of an IRS officer or employee's unreasonable error or delay.

notes.front: A 6404(e)(1) interest abatement claim must be filed within {{c1::3 years of the original filing or 2 years of paying the tax}}, whichever is later.
notes.explanation: This is the first of the six criteria on the IRS interest abatement page.
notes.source: IRS, “Interest abatement”, “Who qualifies for interest abatement”
notes.evidence: File your claim 3 years from when the return was originally filed or 2 years from the payment date of tax, whichever is later.

notes.front: Which type of tax can never get interest abatement for IRS error or delay?
notes.back: Employment taxes.
notes.explanation: The criterion covers interest on income, estate, gift and certain excise taxes only.
notes.source: IRS, “Interest abatement”, “Who qualifies for interest abatement”
notes.evidence: Request must pertain to interest on tax for income, estate, gift and certain excise taxes. You may not request interest abatement on employment taxes.

notes.front: For interest abatement, who must not have contributed to the error or delay?
notes.back: Neither the taxpayer nor the taxpayer’s representative.
notes.explanation: A delay the practitioner caused, such as slow replies, defeats the claim.
notes.source: IRS, “Interest abatement”, “Who qualifies for interest abatement”
notes.evidence: Neither you nor your representative contributed to the error or delay.

notes.front: For interest abatement, what kind of IRS act must the unreasonable error or delay relate to?
notes.back: A ministerial or managerial act.
notes.explanation: This sixth criterion is judged case by case.
notes.source: IRS, “Interest abatement”, “Who qualifies for interest abatement”
notes.evidence: Relate to an unreasonable error or delay that occurred (identified on a case-by-case basis) in relation to our performance of ministerial or managerial acts.

notes.front: How much interest can be abated under 6404(e)(1)?
notes.back: Only the interest that accrues during the period of the unreasonable error or delay.
notes.explanation: Interest on the original underpayment outside that period stays payable.
notes.source: IRS, “Interest abatement”, “How much interest may be abated”
notes.evidence: Under IRC 6404(e)(1) we may only abate the amount of interest that accrues during the period in which the unreasonable error or delay occurred.

notes.front: What are the two ways to request interest abatement for IRS error or delay?
notes.back: Form 843, or a signed letter asking the IRS to reduce the overcharged interest.
notes.explanation: Either way, the IRS asks for a detailed description of when and how it caused the delay or error.
notes.source: IRS, “Interest abatement”, “How to request interest abatement”
notes.evidence: Form 843, Claim for Refund and Request for Abatement PDF or A signed letter requesting that we reduce or adjust the overcharged interest.

notes.front: What is Form 843 used for?
notes.back: To claim a refund or request abatement of certain taxes, penalties, additions to tax, interest and fees.
notes.explanation: Its instructions list penalty relief for reasonable cause and interest abatement under 6404(e)(1) among its uses.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 843 (Rev. December 2024), “Purpose of Form”, p. 1
notes.evidence: certain taxes, penalties, additions to tax, interest, and fees.

notes.front: A client missed the filing deadline because she was in hospital for a month over the due date. She has late-filing penalties in two of the last three years. What relief should her enrolled agent seek?
notes.back: B: reasonable cause relief, with the hospital records.
notes.choices:
A) First Time Abate
B) Reasonable cause relief, with the hospital records
C) Interest abatement under 6404(e)
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: her recent penalties break the clean three-year history FTA needs. C is wrong: 6404(e) covers IRS errors or delays, not the taxpayer’s illness.
notes.explanation: Serious illness is a listed example of reasonable cause, and the IRS asks for hospital records or a doctor’s letter with dates.
notes.source: IRS, “Penalty relief due to reasonable cause”, “Failure to file or pay penalties”
notes.evidence: Death, serious illness or unavoidable absence of the taxpayer or immediate family

notes.front: A client who has filed and paid on time for many years filed his 2024 return two weeks late through simple oversight. What is his most likely route to relief from the failure-to-file penalty?
notes.back: C: First Time Abate.
notes.choices:
A) Reasonable cause, since oversight always qualifies
B) None: late filing penalties cannot be removed
C) First Time Abate
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: mistakes and oversights generally do not count as reasonable cause. B is wrong: failure-to-file penalties are eligible for FTA.
notes.explanation: His clean three-year history is what FTA looks at; the reason for the lateness does not matter.
notes.source: IRS, “Penalty relief due to First Time Abate or other administrative waiver”, “How to qualify for the relief”
notes.evidence: You must have a timely compliance history.

notes.front: A client says his return was late because his bookkeeper forgot to file it, and asks for reasonable cause relief on that ground alone. How should his enrolled agent advise him?
notes.back: A: that ground generally fails, because the taxpayer stays responsible.
notes.choices:
A) That ground generally fails, because the taxpayer stays responsible
B) It qualifies automatically as reliance on a professional
C) He must first file Form 2848 for the bookkeeper
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: reliance on a tax professional is listed as generally not qualifying. C is wrong: a power of attorney has nothing to do with whether the reason qualifies.
notes.explanation: The IRS expects a taxpayer to know what the preparer files and to get proof it was sent on time.
notes.source: IRS, “Penalty relief due to reasonable cause”, “Failure to file or pay penalties”
notes.evidence: You're generally responsible for complying with tax law even if someone else handles your taxes.

notes.front: A client wants reasonable cause relief from an underpayment of estimated tax penalty. What should her enrolled agent tell her?
notes.back: C: reasonable cause does not apply to that penalty; its own relief rules must be used.
notes.choices:
A) File Form 843 citing reasonable cause
B) Ask for First Time Abate instead
C) Reasonable cause does not apply to that penalty; its own relief rules must be used
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: reasonable cause is not available for the estimated tax penalty. B is wrong: FTA covers failure to file, pay and deposit, not the estimated tax penalty.
notes.explanation: The IRS names the estimated tax penalty as one to which reasonable cause does not apply, and points to separate pages for reducing it.
notes.source: IRS, “Penalty relief due to reasonable cause”, “Reasonable cause”
notes.evidence: Reasonable cause doesn't apply to certain penalties such as the estimated tax penalty.

notes.front: During an unagreed examination, an IRS clerk misplaces the case file and the case stalls for months. How is the misplacing classed for interest abatement?
notes.back: B: a managerial act.
notes.choices:
A) A ministerial act
B) A managerial act
C) A general administrative decision
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: losing records is named in the managerial definition, not the ministerial one. C is wrong: general administrative decisions concern how returns are processed overall, not one case.
notes.explanation: The temporary or permanent loss of records is part of the definition of a managerial act.
notes.source: IRS, “Interest abatement”, “Managerial act”
notes.evidence: involving the temporary or permanent loss of records

notes.front: An examination transfer to another office has been approved, but the paperwork then sits unsent for months. How is sending the file classed for interest abatement?
notes.back: A: a ministerial act.
notes.choices:
A) A ministerial act
B) A managerial act
C) A decision on applying tax law
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: no records were lost and no personnel judgment is involved. C is wrong: the transfer applies no tax law.
notes.explanation: Once every prerequisite, including approval, is complete, carrying out the step is procedural and involves no discretion.
notes.source: IRS, “Interest abatement”, “Ministerial act”
notes.evidence: A ministerial act is a procedural or mechanical act that does not involve the exercise of judgment or discretion

notes.front: An examiner asks the Office of Chief Counsel for advice on a disputed deduction, and the answer takes a year. Can the client get the interest for that year abated?
notes.back: C: no, because a decision to request legal advice applies tax law.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, as a ministerial delay
B) Yes, as a managerial delay
C) No, because a decision to request legal advice applies tax law
notes.choicesExplained: A and B are wrong: a decision on the proper application of tax law is neither ministerial nor managerial.
notes.explanation: Only delays in ministerial or managerial acts qualify under 6404(e)(1).
notes.source: IRS, “Interest abatement”, “Managerial act examples”
notes.evidence: The decision to request advice is a decision concerning the proper application of federal tax law; it is neither a ministerial nor a managerial act.

notes.front: An employer client blames an IRS delay for interest on its Form 941 employment tax balance, and the delay began after the IRS wrote to it. Can its enrolled agent get that interest abated under 6404(e)(1)?
notes.back: B: no, because employment taxes are excluded.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, because the delay followed written contact
B) No, because employment taxes are excluded
C) Yes, but only by phone
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: meeting one criterion is not enough; all six must be met. C is wrong: requests are made on Form 843 or by signed letter, and none would succeed here.
notes.explanation: The criteria confine abatement to interest on income, estate, gift and certain excise taxes.
notes.source: IRS, “Interest abatement”, “Who qualifies for interest abatement”
notes.evidence: You may not request interest abatement on employment taxes.

notes.front: A client whose return was picked by random sample fears the IRS thinks she cheated. What should her enrolled agent tell her?
notes.back: C: selection does not suggest an error or dishonesty.
notes.choices:
A) Selection means the IRS has found an error
B) Selection means a penalty will follow
C) Selection does not suggest an error or dishonesty
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: returns are also chosen by screening and random sample, not only for errors found. B is wrong: an examination can end with no change proposed.
notes.explanation: Publication 556 says selection does not suggest the taxpayer made an error or is dishonest.
notes.source: Publication 556, Examination of Returns, Appeal Rights, and Claims for Refund (Rev. September 2013), “Introduction”, p. 1
notes.evidence: If your return is selected for examination, it does not

notes.front: Returns are chosen for examination by computerized screening, by {{c1::random sample}}, or by an income document matching program.
notes.explanation: Publication 556 also mentions market-segment studies and tips from other sources.
notes.source: Publication 556, Examination of Returns, Appeal Rights, and Claims for Refund (Rev. September 2013), “Introduction”, p. 1
notes.evidence: are chosen by computerized screening, by random

notes.front: Where can an examination not handled by mail take place?
notes.back: At the taxpayer’s home or business, an IRS office, or the office of the authorised representative.
notes.explanation: Publication 556 lists these four places for in-person examinations.
notes.source: Publication 556, Examination of Returns, Appeal Rights, and Claims for Refund (Rev. September 2013), “If Your Return Is Examined”, p. 3
notes.evidence: your place of business, an Internal Revenue office, or the

notes.front: Under section 7605(a), what time and place of examination applies?
notes.back: One fixed by the Secretary that is reasonable under the circumstances.
notes.explanation: The statute gives the IRS the choice but ties it to reasonableness.
notes.source: 26 U.S.C. § 7605, Time and place of examination, “(a) Time and place”
notes.evidence: shall be such time and place as may be fixed by the Secretary and as are reasonable under the circumstances

notes.front: How many inspections of a taxpayer’s books may the IRS make for each taxable year?
notes.back: Only one, unless the taxpayer asks otherwise or the IRS notifies the taxpayer in writing that another is necessary.
notes.explanation: Section 7605(b) also bars unnecessary examinations or investigations.
notes.source: 26 U.S.C. § 7605, Time and place of examination, “(b) Restrictions on examination of taxpayer”
notes.evidence: only one inspection of a taxpayer's books of account shall be made for each taxable year unless the taxpayer requests otherwise or unless the Secretary, after investigation, notifies the taxpayer in writing that an additional inspection is necessary

notes.front: Under section 7602(a)(1), what may the IRS examine?
notes.back: Any books, papers, records or other data that may be relevant or material to the inquiry.
notes.explanation: The power serves purposes such as checking a return’s correctness, making a return where none was filed, and collecting tax.
notes.source: 26 U.S.C. § 7602, Examination of books and witnesses, “(a) Authority to summon, etc.”
notes.evidence: To examine any books, papers, records, or other data which may be relevant or material to such inquiry

notes.front: Under section 7521(b)(2), what must the IRS do if a taxpayer clearly asks during an interview to consult a representative?
notes.back: Suspend the interview, even if the taxpayer has already answered some questions.
notes.explanation: The right covers consulting an attorney, certified public accountant, enrolled agent, enrolled actuary or other permitted representative.
notes.source: 26 U.S.C. § 7521, Procedures involving taxpayer interviews, “(b)(2) Right of consultation”
notes.evidence: such officer or employee shall suspend such interview regardless of whether the taxpayer may have answered one or more questions

notes.front: Can the IRS require a taxpayer to come to an interview with the representative?
notes.back: Not unless an administrative summons has been issued to the taxpayer.
notes.explanation: The representative must hold a written power of attorney and not be disbarred or suspended.
notes.source: 26 U.S.C. § 7521, Procedures involving taxpayer interviews, “(c) Representatives holding power of attorney”
notes.evidence: An officer or employee of the Internal Revenue Service may not require a taxpayer to accompany the representative in the absence of an administrative summons issued to the taxpayer

notes.front: What protection does section 7525 give communications with a federally authorized tax practitioner?
notes.back: For tax advice, the same common law confidentiality that protects taxpayer–attorney communications.
notes.explanation: It applies only to the extent the communication would be privileged if it were with an attorney.
notes.source: 26 U.S.C. § 7525, Confidentiality privileges relating to taxpayer communications, “(a)(1) General rule”
notes.evidence: the same common law protections of confidentiality which apply to a communication between a taxpayer and an attorney shall also apply to a communication between a taxpayer and any federally authorized tax practitioner

notes.front: In which matters can the 7525 privilege be asserted?
notes.back: Noncriminal tax matters before the IRS and noncriminal tax proceedings in federal court by or against the United States.
notes.explanation: Section 7525(a)(2) limits the privilege to these two settings, so criminal matters fall outside it.
notes.source: 26 U.S.C. § 7525, Confidentiality privileges relating to taxpayer communications, “(a)(2) Limitations”
notes.evidence: any noncriminal tax matter before the Internal Revenue Service; and (B) any noncriminal tax proceeding in Federal court brought by or against the United States

notes.front: Which written communications are excluded from the 7525 privilege?
notes.back: Those made in connection with promoting a person’s participation in a tax shelter.
notes.explanation: Section 7525(b) removes the privilege for written tax shelter promotion, whoever in the business receives it.
notes.source: 26 U.S.C. § 7525, Confidentiality privileges relating to taxpayer communications, “(b) Section not to apply to communications regarding tax shelters”
notes.evidence: in connection with the promotion of the direct or indirect participation of the person in any tax shelter

notes.front: How does a taxpayer learn which records to bring to an examination?
notes.back: The IRS says which records will be needed.
notes.explanation: Publication 556 notes the examination proceeds more easily if records are gathered before any interview.
notes.source: Publication 556, Examination of Returns, Appeal Rights, and Claims for Refund (Rev. September 2013), “The Examination”, p. 4
notes.evidence: your return has been selected. The IRS will tell you which

notes.front: Besides credible evidence, what must a taxpayer have done for the burden of proof to shift under 7491(a)?
notes.back: Met the substantiation rules, kept all required records, and cooperated with reasonable IRS requests.
notes.explanation: A partnership, corporation or trust must also meet a net worth limit under 7430.
notes.source: 26 U.S.C. § 7491, Burden of proof, “(a)(2) Limitations”
notes.evidence: the taxpayer has complied with the requirements under this title to substantiate any item; (B) the taxpayer has maintained all records required under this title and has cooperated with reasonable requests by the Secretary

notes.front: What does a taxpayer who agrees with an examiner’s proposed changes do?
notes.back: Signs an agreement form and pays any additional tax owed, plus interest.
notes.explanation: Most taxpayers agree, and the examination closes at that level.
notes.source: Publication 556, Examination of Returns, Appeal Rights, and Claims for Refund (Rev. September 2013), “If You Agree”, p. 4
notes.evidence: If you agree with the proposed changes, you can sign an

notes.front: If a taxpayer disagrees at an examination held in an IRS office, what can be requested at once?
notes.back: An immediate meeting with the examiner’s supervisor.
notes.explanation: If agreement is reached there, the case closes; if not, the examiner writes up both positions.
notes.source: Publication 556, Examination of Returns, Appeal Rights, and Claims for Refund (Rev. September 2013), “If You Do Not Agree”, p. 4
notes.evidence: takes place in an IRS office, you can request an

notes.front: Besides the 30-day letter, what document in the package explains the examiner’s proposed changes?
notes.back: A copy of the examination report.
notes.explanation: The package also holds an agreement or waiver form and a copy of Publication 5.
notes.source: Publication 556, Examination of Returns, Appeal Rights, and Claims for Refund (Rev. September 2013), “30-day letter and 90-day letter”, p. 5
notes.evidence: A copy of the examination report explaining the exam

notes.front: Midway through an in-person audit interview she attended voluntarily, a client says clearly that she wants to speak to her enrolled agent before answering more. What must the revenue agent do?
notes.back: A: suspend the interview.
notes.choices:
A) Suspend the interview
B) Finish the questions already started
C) Continue, because she has already answered some questions
notes.choicesExplained: B and C are wrong: the interview must be suspended regardless of whether she has answered some questions.
notes.explanation: Only an interview started by an administrative summons is outside the right of consultation, and this one was voluntary.
notes.source: 26 U.S.C. § 7521, Procedures involving taxpayer interviews, “(b)(2) Right of consultation”
notes.evidence: such officer or employee shall suspend such interview regardless of whether the taxpayer may have answered one or more questions

notes.front: An enrolled agent with a valid Form 2848 arrives alone for a field examination. No summons has been issued. The revenue agent insists the client must attend too. Is that right?
notes.back: C: no; the IRS may not require the taxpayer to accompany the representative.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, taxpayers must always attend the first meeting
B) Yes, unless the enrolled agent prepared the return
C) No; the IRS may not require the taxpayer to accompany the representative
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: 7521(c) sets no such first-meeting rule. B is wrong: who prepared the return is irrelevant to this rule.
notes.explanation: Only an administrative summons issued to the taxpayer allows the IRS to require attendance.
notes.source: 26 U.S.C. § 7521, Procedures involving taxpayer interviews, “(c) Representatives holding power of attorney”
notes.evidence: may not require a taxpayer to accompany the representative in the absence of an administrative summons

notes.front: An enrolled agent’s client becomes the subject of a criminal tax investigation. Can the enrolled agent rely on the 7525 privilege to protect their past tax advice?
notes.back: B: no; 7525 applies only in noncriminal matters.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, as for any attorney–client communication
B) No; 7525 applies only in noncriminal matters
C) Yes, if the advice was in writing
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: the 7525 privilege is limited to noncriminal settings. C is wrong: written form does not extend it, and written tax shelter promotion is expressly excluded.
notes.explanation: Section 7525(a)(2) lists only noncriminal IRS matters and noncriminal federal court proceedings.
notes.source: 26 U.S.C. § 7525, Confidentiality privileges relating to taxpayer communications, “(a)(2) Limitations”
notes.evidence: Paragraph (1) may only be asserted in- (A) any noncriminal tax matter before the Internal Revenue Service

notes.front: Months after closing a client’s 2023 examination, the IRS asks to inspect the same year’s books again, without any written notice. What can the client’s enrolled agent point to?
notes.back: A: 7605(b): only one inspection per year unless the IRS gives written notice that another is necessary.
notes.choices:
A) 7605(b): only one inspection per year unless the IRS gives written notice that another is necessary
B) 7521: the right to record interviews
C) 7491: the burden of proof
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: recording rights do not limit repeat inspections. C is wrong: the burden of proof applies in court, not to the number of inspections.
notes.explanation: Section 7605(b) also protects against unnecessary examinations or investigations.
notes.source: 26 U.S.C. § 7605, Time and place of examination, “(b) Restrictions on examination of taxpayer”
notes.evidence: No taxpayer shall be subjected to unnecessary examination or investigations

notes.front: In a Tax Court case, a client offers credible evidence on a deduction but never kept the records the Code requires for it. Does the burden of proof shift to the IRS on that issue?
notes.back: C: no, because the record-keeping condition is not met.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, credible evidence alone shifts it
B) Yes, the IRS always bears the burden in court
C) No, because the record-keeping condition is not met
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: 7491(a)(2) adds conditions to credible evidence. B is wrong: the burden shifts only issue by issue, when the conditions are met.
notes.explanation: The taxpayer must also meet substantiation rules and cooperate with reasonable requests.
notes.source: 26 U.S.C. § 7491, Burden of proof, “(a)(2) Limitations”
notes.evidence: the taxpayer has maintained all records required under this title

notes.front: A client receives a letter asking him to post copies of receipts for his charitable deductions. No meeting is proposed. What kind of examination is this?
notes.back: B: an examination handled by mail.
notes.choices:
A) A field examination
B) An examination handled by mail
C) Not an examination, because no one visits
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: a field examination happens in person at the home or business. C is wrong: Publication 556 counts mail examinations as examinations.
notes.explanation: Publication 556 says some examinations are handled entirely by mail.
notes.source: Publication 556, Examination of Returns, Appeal Rights, and Claims for Refund (Rev. September 2013), “If Your Return Is Examined”, p. 3
notes.evidence: Some examinations are handled entirely by mail.

notes.front: After an office audit, a client disagrees with the examiner. The supervisor meeting fails and a 30-day letter arrives. What are the client’s options within the 30 days?
notes.back: A: accept the changes, or appeal them following the letter.
notes.choices:
A) Accept the changes, or appeal them following the letter
B) Only petition the Tax Court at once
C) Ignore it until the tax is billed
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: the Tax Court petition follows the notice of deficiency, not the 30-day letter. C is wrong: ignoring it leads to a notice of deficiency, not a simple bill.
notes.explanation: Publication 556 gives about 30 days from the letter to say whether the taxpayer will accept or appeal.
notes.source: Publication 556, Examination of Returns, Appeal Rights, and Claims for Refund (Rev. September 2013), “30-day letter and 90-day letter”, p. 5
notes.evidence: You generally have 30 days from the date of the 30-day

notes.front: How many levels of administrative appeal are there within the IRS?
notes.back: One: Appeals is the only level.
notes.explanation: Publication 5 describes Appeals as independent and separate from the IRS division that proposed the changes.
notes.source: Publication 5, Your Appeal Rights and How To Prepare a Protest If You Disagree (Rev. 4-2021), “IRS Independent Office of Appeals”, p. 4
notes.evidence: the changes. It is the only level of administrative

notes.front: What does Publication 5 say about how most disputes end at Appeals?
notes.back: Most can be settled informally at the Appeals level without litigation.
notes.explanation: Appeals weighs both sides’ arguments and applies the tax law, including court decisions, to the facts.
notes.source: Publication 5, Your Appeal Rights and How To Prepare a Protest If You Disagree (Rev. 4-2021), “IRS Independent Office of Appeals”, p. 4
notes.evidence: Most disputes can be settled informally at the

notes.front: Per Publication 5 (2021), when is a formal written protest required because of the amount?
notes.back: When the proposed change in tax and penalties for any tax period is more than $25,000.
notes.explanation: The total counts the proposed increase or decrease in tax and penalties, or the claimed refund.
notes.source: Publication 5, Your Appeal Rights and How To Prepare a Protest If You Disagree (Rev. 4-2021), “Formal Written Protest”, p. 4
notes.evidence: for any tax period is more than $25,000 in the

notes.front: For each disputed issue, what two kinds of support does a formal protest set out?
notes.back: The facts supporting the taxpayer’s position, and the law or authority, if any, supporting it.
notes.explanation: The protest also lists the disputed issues, periods, proposed changes and reasons for disagreeing.
notes.source: Publication 5, Your Appeal Rights and How To Prepare a Protest If You Disagree (Rev. 4-2021), “Formal Written Protest”, p. 4
notes.evidence: Facts supporting your position on each

notes.front: What declaration must a formal protest contain, signed by the taxpayer or representative?
notes.back: A penalties of perjury statement.
notes.explanation: Publication 5 gives the exact wording to use.
notes.source: Publication 5, Your Appeal Rights and How To Prepare a Protest If You Disagree (Rev. 4-2021), “Formal Written Protest”, p. 4
notes.evidence: Penalties of perjury statement, as follows:

notes.front: Who may represent a taxpayer at an Appeals conference?
notes.back: A person authorised to practise before Appeals, such as an attorney, certified public accountant or enrolled agent.
notes.explanation: Publication 5 points to Circular 230 for the qualifications to practise before Appeals.
notes.source: Publication 5, Your Appeal Rights and How To Prepare a Protest If You Disagree (Rev. 4-2021), “The Appeals Conference”, p. 5
notes.evidence: accountant, or enrolled agent. See Circular No.

notes.front: What must be filed for a representative attending an Appeals conference alone to receive confidential information?
notes.back: A power of attorney or a tax information authorisation.
notes.explanation: Publication 556 accepts Form 2848 or another properly written authorisation.
notes.source: Publication 556, Examination of Returns, Appeal Rights, and Claims for Refund (Rev. September 2013), “Representation”, p. 9
notes.evidence: only if you have filed a power of attorney or a tax

notes.front: How long after a notice of deficiency is mailed does a taxpayer have to petition the Tax Court?
notes.back: 90 days, or 150 days if the notice is addressed to a person outside the United States.
notes.explanation: If the last day is a weekend or District of Columbia holiday, it does not count as the last day.
notes.source: 26 U.S.C. § 6213, Restrictions applicable to deficiencies; petition to Tax Court, “(a) Time for filing petition and restriction on assessment”
notes.evidence: Within 90 days, or 150 days if the notice is addressed to a person outside the United States, after the notice of deficiency authorized in section 6212 is mailed

notes.front: Can the IRS assess a deficiency while the 90-day petition period is running?
notes.back: No; nor, if a petition is filed, until the Tax Court decision is final.
notes.explanation: Section 6213(a) also bars levy or court proceedings for collection during that time, except as other sections provide.
notes.source: 26 U.S.C. § 6213, Restrictions applicable to deficiencies; petition to Tax Court, “(a) Time for filing petition and restriction on assessment”
notes.evidence: nor until the expiration of such 90-day or 150-day period, as the case may be, nor, if a petition has been filed with the Tax Court, until the decision of the Tax Court has become final

notes.front: Per Publication 556 (2013), what amount allows a Tax Court case to use the small tax case procedure?
notes.back: $50,000 or less for any one tax year or period.
notes.explanation: If the court agrees, its decision is final and cannot be appealed.
notes.source: Publication 556, Examination of Returns, Appeal Rights, and Claims for Refund (Rev. September 2013), “Tax Court”, p. 12
notes.evidence: $50,000 or less for any 1 tax year or period, you can re

notes.front: Before going to a District Court or the Court of Federal Claims, what must a taxpayer generally have done?
notes.back: Paid the full amount and timely filed a claim for refund with the IRS.
notes.explanation: These courts hear refund suits, unlike the Tax Court, which hears cases before payment.
notes.source: Publication 5, Your Appeal Rights and How To Prepare a Protest If You Disagree (Rev. 4-2021), “District Court and the U.S. Court of Federal Claims”, p. 6
notes.evidence: only after you have fully paid the amount and timely

notes.front: An examination of an individual proposes $31,000 of extra tax and penalties for 2023 and $4,000 for 2024. The client wants Appeals. What must his enrolled agent file (Pub 5, 2021)?
notes.back: C: a formal written protest covering both years.
notes.choices:
A) A small case request for 2024 and a protest for 2023
B) A small case request for both years
C) A formal written protest covering both years
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: once any period exceeds $25,000, every period needs the formal protest. B is wrong: 2023 is over the $25,000 limit.
notes.explanation: Publication 5 requires a formal written protest for all periods when any one of them exceeds the threshold.
notes.source: Publication 5, Your Appeal Rights and How To Prepare a Protest If You Disagree (Rev. 4-2021), “Formal Written Protest”, p. 4
notes.evidence: protest for all periods involved.

notes.front: An S corporation disputes $9,000 of proposed changes and wants an Appeals conference. What does it need to file?
notes.back: A: a formal written protest.
notes.choices:
A) A formal written protest
B) A small case request, since the amount is low
C) Nothing; Appeals will call
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: S corporation cases need a formal protest whatever the amount. C is wrong: a written request is needed to reach Appeals.
notes.explanation: Partnership and S corporation cases are named as needing a formal protest regardless of the dollar amount.
notes.source: Publication 5, Your Appeal Rights and How To Prepare a Protest If You Disagree (Rev. 4-2021), “Formal Written Protest”, p. 4
notes.evidence: Partnership and S Corporation cases

notes.front: A notice of deficiency is mailed to a client at her address in Germany. How long does she have to petition the Tax Court?
notes.back: B: 150 days.
notes.choices:
A) 90 days
B) 150 days
C) 30 days
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: 90 days applies to notices addressed inside the United States. C is wrong: 30 days is the response time on a 30-day letter.
notes.explanation: Section 6213(a) gives 150 days when the notice is addressed to a person outside the United States.
notes.source: 26 U.S.C. § 6213, Restrictions applicable to deficiencies; petition to Tax Court, “(a) Time for filing petition and restriction on assessment”
notes.evidence: or 150 days if the notice is addressed to a person outside the United States

notes.front: A client who received a notice of deficiency wants a judge to hear her case but cannot pay the tax first. Which court should she use?
notes.back: A: the U.S. Tax Court.
notes.choices:
A) The U.S. Tax Court
B) A U.S. District Court
C) The U.S. Court of Federal Claims
notes.choicesExplained: B and C are wrong: those courts generally hear a case only after full payment and a timely refund claim.
notes.explanation: The Tax Court is generally a prepayment forum, and the notice of deficiency gives her the right to petition it.
notes.source: Publication 5, Your Appeal Rights and How To Prepare a Protest If You Disagree (Rev. 4-2021), “U.S. Tax Court”, p. 5
notes.evidence: Tax Court before making full payment, but its

notes.front: Eighty days after a notice of deficiency, a client is still negotiating with Appeals and assumes the petition deadline is paused. What should her enrolled agent tell her?
notes.back: C: the deadline keeps running; petition the Tax Court in time.
notes.choices:
A) The deadline pauses while Appeals is involved
B) Appeals can extend the deadline on request
C) The deadline keeps running; petition the Tax Court in time
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: talking to examiners or Appeals does not stop the clock. B is wrong: neither the IRS nor the Tax Court can change the period.
notes.explanation: Publication 5 says the law sets the petition period and it runs even during talks with the IRS.
notes.source: Publication 5, Your Appeal Rights and How To Prepare a Protest If You Disagree (Rev. 4-2021), “U.S. Tax Court”, p. 6
notes.evidence: court, even if you continue to talk to IRS examiners

notes.front: A client wants his enrolled agent to argue at Appeals that income tax is unconstitutional. What will Appeals do with that argument?
notes.back: B: not consider it, since Appeals considers only arguments based on tax law.
notes.choices:
A) Refer it to the Tax Court
B) Not consider it, since Appeals considers only arguments based on tax law
C) Settle half the case to avoid litigation
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: Appeals does not refer arguments to the court. C is wrong: settlement comes from applying tax law to the facts, not from splitting a baseless claim.
notes.explanation: Publication 5 says Appeals cannot consider constitutional or similar objections to paying tax.
notes.source: Publication 5, Your Appeal Rights and How To Prepare a Protest If You Disagree (Rev. 4-2021), “IRS Independent Office of Appeals”, p. 4
notes.evidence: your arguments if they are based only on moral,

notes.front: How do the small case request at Appeals and the Tax Court small tax case differ in their limits?
notes.back: Appeals small case request: $25,000 or less per period. Tax Court small tax case: $50,000 or less per year (both Pub 556, 2013).
notes.explanation: They are different forums: one replaces a formal protest, the other simplifies a court case with no appeal.
notes.source: Publication 556, Examination of Returns, Appeal Rights, and Claims for Refund (Rev. September 2013), “Protests and Small Case Requests”, p. 9
notes.evidence: riod is not more than $25,000, you may make a small case

notes.front: How does a 30-day letter differ from a 90-day letter?
notes.back: The 30-day letter offers an administrative appeal of proposed changes; the 90-day letter is the notice of deficiency opening the Tax Court route.
notes.explanation: The 90-day letter follows when the 30-day letter goes unanswered or Appeals reaches no agreement.
notes.source: Publication 556, Examination of Returns, Appeal Rights, and Claims for Refund (Rev. September 2013), “30-day letter and 90-day letter”, p. 5
notes.evidence: is also known as a notice of deficiency.

notes.front: How does interest abatement under 6404(e) differ from reasonable cause penalty relief?
notes.back: 6404(e) turns on the IRS’s own unreasonable error or delay; reasonable cause turns on the taxpayer’s care and good faith.
notes.explanation: Under 6404(e) the taxpayer must not have contributed to the delay, so the fault lies with the IRS.
notes.source: IRS, “Interest abatement”, “Interest abatement”
notes.evidence: the IRS may reduce the amount of interest you owe if the interest is applied because of an IRS officer or employee's unreasonable error or delay

notes.front: What separates a ministerial act from a managerial act?
notes.back: A ministerial act involves no judgment; a managerial act involves lost records or judgment in managing personnel.
notes.explanation: Both can support interest abatement, but a decision on applying tax law is neither.
notes.source: IRS, “Interest abatement”, “Managerial act”
notes.evidence: exercise of judgment or discretion relating to management of personnel
